PROJECT SUMMARY – PROJECT 3
Sickle cell disease (SCD) and α-thalassemia (AT) are among the most common inherited blood disorders
worldwide, causing severe anemia, organ dysfunction, and early death. Although ex vivo CRISPR or base editing
of autologous hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) with transplantation has shown promise, these methods are limited
by the need for HSC harvesting, myeloablation, and specialized facilities, which restrict accessibility and
practicality. A transformative alternative is in vivo HSC editing, delivered prenatally, which could overcome these
barriers and prevent disease before irreversible damage occurs.
This project tests the hypothesis that systemic in utero delivery of optimized lipid nanoparticles (LNP) carrying
base editor mRNA can effectively target fetal HSC in the liver, enabling lasting gene correction for SCD and AT.
The fetal environment offers unique biological benefits, including immune tolerance, a small size that maximizes
dose-to-weight ratio, and hematopoiesis occurring in the liver, a natural site for LNP uptake. Preliminary data
show improved delivery of mRNA and CRISPR editing to fetal HSCs in mice, as well as successful in utero
editing in sheep and non-human primate (NHP) models.
Specific Aim 1 will refine LNP formulations, both naked and targeted (anti-CD117 and anti-CD45 conjugates),
to enhance in utero HSC delivery and editing in mouse models of SCD and AT. This includes correcting the Hb
Constant Spring (HbCs) variant and introducing the non-pathogenic Makassar β-globin variant.
Specific Aim 2 will apply these techniques to preclinical large-animal models, assessing optimized LNP in fetal
sheep for biodistribution and safety, and conducting in utero adenine base editing in NHPs to induce fetal γ-
globin expression.
By building on strong preliminary data and collaborating with core facilities, this project aims to establish the
feasibility, safety, and potential for translation of prenatal in vivo HSC editing. Success will lay the groundwork
for first-in-human in utero gene-editing trials for hemoglobinopathies and guide therapies for other genetic blood
disorders.

PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT
The objective of the proposed project is to further develop an enabling, platform technology to help
researchers more easily isolate cells of interest from blood samples. While major feasibility gaps have
already been overcome, additional work on these cell separation devices is required to translate the current
pilot prototype design into a mass-manufacturable embodiment which still retains the unprecedented
capabilities that have been established to date. These include removal of ~99% of red blood cells and
platelets from whole blood samples, as well as the separation of ~95% monocytes and granulocytes from
the lymphocyte / stem cell population. The ability to process standard whole blood draws – rather than
depending on expensive units of mononuclear cells that were harvested via leukapheresis, or the purchase
of frozen aliquots of these units – to acquire the initial starting material with which to perform R&D on
cellular therapies would foster research in the basic, translational, and clinical sciences related to a variety
of blood diseases and disorders. These include, for example, the acquisition of (i) peripheral blood stem
cells in order to perform CRISPR-style research on sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, and other inherited
blood disorders, (ii) monocytes with which to perform extracorporeal photopheresis to investigate or treat
an array of different conditions, including graft versus host disease and cutaneous T cell lymphoma, and
(iii) lymphocytes for the development of adoptive cell-based therapies. The proposed project is aimed at
increasing the readiness level of the novel flow-through cell separation technology described, by first
producing thermoplastic device prototypes, to be manufactured via high-volume commercial techniques,
and then validating in particular their ability to concentrate the CD34+ stem cell population in whole blood
samples by ~100X, while processing an entire 500mL unit of cold-stored whole blood in 2 hours. Single-
use thermoplastic devices will be driven by a basic, off-the-shelf peristaltic pump as with prior prototypes,
which further ensures this platform technology will be amenable to widespread adoption, without the
significant equipment cost expenditure required by existing automated methods. The ‘debulking’ of whole
blood samples, to remove the overwhelming number of interfering cells (largely red cells and platelets) and
enable the selection of rarer cells of interest, while seemingly a simple task is in reality a significant
challenge – one which presently has no ready solution that does not involve undesirable chemical
gradients or lysis steps. A transformative methodology that is wholly different from the inadequate,
currently-available approaches is needed in order to improve the pace and quality of groundbreaking R&D
efforts, and help enable cell-based therapies to fulfill their immense potential.
results.project_title: Development and validation of a cell separation platform technology
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
A flow-through device module, which is capable of efficiently concentrating cells of interest from a sample
of whole blood (or other cell source), will be evaluated against benchmark performance metrics, as it is
transitioned from lab-scale prototypes to mass-production. The same device which will enrich peripheral
blood stem cells and lymphocytes for research on cellular therapies can also be used, for example, in
situations where a concentrated output of monocytes is required, for the detection of circulating tumor cells,
or for simply washing/formulating cells that have been cultured, among many other potential applications.
Such an enabling platform technology, once rigorously validated, would ease the logistical, sterility, and
quality concerns associated with conventional approaches to blood cell isolation – which typically employ
cell-damaging chemical steps and/or centrifugation – and enable cells of interest to be harvested by
researchers more easily and less expensively.

PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Sickle cell disease (SCD) causes substantial neurovascular morbidity in childhood. Silent cerebral
infarcts (SCI) are the most common neurological complication, impairing cognition, and increase
future stroke risk, yet there is no repeatable and inexpensive method to monitor SCI between
infrequent MRIs. The retina offers a direct view of microvascular health. Sickle cell maculopathy
(SCM) on OCT and OCT-A captures temporal parafoveal vulnerability that may mirror SCI-prone
deep white matter watershed zones that are vulnerable to sci. Our long-term goal is to establish
quantitative macular metrics as noninvasive biomarkers that detect current SCI, forecast incident
SCI, and track response to disease-modifying therapy in pediatric SCD. We will conduct a
prospective cohort study of 80 children with SCD, ages 6 to 18 years, who will undergo annual
OCT/OCT-A and an exit brain MRI. Aim 1 will test the cross-sectional association between SCI
on clinical MRI and macular measures including temporal deep capillary plexus vessel density,
temporal parafoveal inner-retinal thickness, and foveal avascular zone area, using eye-level
models that account for inter-eye correlation and adjust for genotype, hemolysis profile, and
treatment exposure. Aim 2 will determine whether baseline macular status and longitudinal slopes
of these measures predict incident SCI at the exit. Aim 3 will evaluate whether cumulative
exposure to hydroxyurea or chronic red cell exchange transfusion is associated with slower
progression of SCM using time-updated analyses. The expected outcome is a set of validated,
clinic-ready retinal endpoints and a risk score that enable noninvasive surveillance for SCI and
inform timing of neuroprotective therapy. This multidisciplinary project leverages pediatric
hematology, neuroradiology, and retinal imaging expertise to deliver a scalable approach that can
be expanded to multi-site validation and ultimately integrated into routine care for children with
SCD.
results.project_title: Association of Retinal Perfusion with Cerebral Microvascular Injury in Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
This project will establish the retina, measured with OCT and OCT A, as a practical indicator of
cerebral microvascular health in children with sickle cell disease. The data will produce a retinal
risk score, clear cut points for key measures, and a clinic protocol for screening and follow up.
The knowledge gained will enable retinal imaging a standard part of pediatric sickle cell care that
guides MRI timing and therapy to prevent silent brain injury and preserve cognition.

PROJECT ABSTRACT – OVERALL
This Program Project Grant (PPG) aims to develop safe, effective, and scalable curative therapies for
hemoglobinopathies (including sickle cell disease (SCD), a-thalassemia (AT), and b-thalassemia (BT)) and
Fanconi anemia (FA) by targeting hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) in vivo. While hematopoietic stem cell
transplantation (HSCT) can be curative, the toxicities associated with current conditioning regimens limit eligibility
and threaten fertility and long-term health. The heavy strain placed on patients, families, and healthcare systems,
spanning inpatient care, emergency services, transfusions, and long-term complication management, highlights
the pressing need for innovative, safer, and more widely accessible curative treatments. Our comprehensive and
integrated research strategy brings together cutting-edge technologies and innovative methodologies to address
HSC disorders. Specifically, we employ antibody-directed, HSC-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNP) designed to
deliver mRNA-encoded pro-apoptotic (PA) payloads or gene editors directly to diseased stem cells. This precise
delivery system is coupled with advanced disease modeling platforms, including humanized mouse models and
preclinical large animal systems such as sheep and non-human primates, to rigorously evaluate both safety and
efficacy. The ultimate goal is to achieve either the selective depletion of diseased populations or durable genetic
correction of faulty HSC, paving the way for transformative therapies. Supporting this approach are three
interconnected research projects, which are reinforced by two specialized scientific cores and a central
administrative core. Together, these components ensure scientific rigor, foster collaboration and synergy across
teams, and enable rapid iterative cycles of discovery, refinement, and translation toward clinical application.
Project 1 improves fertility-preserving conditioning through targeted HSC depletion and develops in vivo gene
editing for hemoglobinopathies. Project 2 explores interhomolog recombination for allele repair and non-toxic in
vivo selection in FA. Project 3 focuses on prenatal LNP-mediated base editing of fetal HSC to intervene before
disease begins. Core B (Optimized Nucleic Acid and Cell-Specific Delivery) designs and produces HSC-targeted
LNP and continuously improves formulations based on project feedback. Core C (Gene Editing, iPSC, and HSC)
supplies editing platforms, iPSC-derived HSPCs, and humanized xenograft models; Core A (Administrative)
manages governance, compliance, data sharing, and evaluation. Innovation involves in situ HSC editing and
conditioning using antibody-functionalized LNP, prenatal delivery to the fetal liver HSC niche, and careful
measurement of on- and off-target effects across species. Anticipated outcomes include fertility-preserving
transplant conditioning, effective in vivo correction of disease alleles, and robust preclinical evidence to mitigate
risks in translation. By reducing toxicity, simplifying procedures, and enabling earlier intervention, this program
aims to expand access to curative therapies and lay the groundwork for first-in-human studies.

This Program Project Grant will develop safer and more accessible cures for inherited blood disorders, including
sickle cell disease, beta-thalassemia, alpha-thalassemia, and Fanconi anemia. By combining lipid nanoparticles
that directly deliver gene-editing tools to blood stem cells with advanced preclinical models, the program aims to
reduce the toxic side effects of current treatments and make curative therapies available to more patients. These
studies will generate the knowledge and tools needed to advance innovative in vivo and prenatal gene therapy
approaches toward the clinic, ultimately improving survival and quality of life for children and adults living with
these severe conditions.

ABSTRACT
Red blood cell (RBC) transfusions are critical in the management of inherited RBC disorders, trauma, and
neonatal care, but they are not without risk. Alloimmunization—the development of antibodies against donor
RBC antigens—is a serious complication that disproportionately affects individuals with sickle cell disease
(SCD) due to frequent transfusions and genetic variation in the Rh blood group system, leading to increased
morbidity, limited transfusion options, and delayed care. Precise alloantibody identification requires access to
reagent RBCs with rare or variant antigen profiles, which are in extremely limited supply. In parallel, recent
clinical data suggest that transfusing fetal-type RBCs, such as cord blood RBCs, may reduce complications
like retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) in very premature infants, but supply limitations hinder their clinical use.
These challenges highlight an urgent need for a renewable, scalable, and customizable source of RBCs
tailored to the diagnostic and therapeutic needs of vulnerable patient populations.
The goal of this project is to engineer and scale the production of RBCs from human induced pluripotent stem
cells (iPSCs)—termed iRBCs—for two high-impact applications: alloantibody detection and neonatal
transfusion. Building on complementary expertise in gene editing, erythroid differentiation, and transfusion
biology, the project combines advanced differentiation methods with genome engineering to produce definitive
iRBCs with rare blood group antigen profiles and fetal-type functional characteristics. In Aim 1, we will define
the molecular and metabolic programs that govern blood group antigen expression, maturation, and function in
definitive iRBCs, and assess their utility in antibody detection and in vivo survival. In Aim 2, we will optimize
the scalable production of definitive iRBCs by enhancing hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell (HSPC)
generation, erythroid lineage commitment, and yield through culture optimization and targeted gene editing.
This work addresses two major unmet needs in transfusion medicine: the lack of reagent RBCs with rare or
variant antigen profiles to support alloantibody diagnosis in patients with SCD, and the absence of a scalable
source of fetal-type RBCs for neonatal transfusion. By generating clinically relevant, developmentally matched
iRBCs, this project has the potential to establish a transformative platform for personalized transfusion support
and significantly improve outcomes for both SCD patients and premature infants.

NARRATIVE
Red blood cell transfusions are lifesaving but can cause serious complications, especially in patients with sickle
cell disease and premature infants. This project aims to develop a scalable source of red blood cells from human
pluripotent stem cells that are tailored for two critical clinical needs: identifying complex antibodies in transfusion-
dependent patients and providing safer, fetal-type red cells for premature neonates. These innovations have the
potential to improve transfusion safety, diagnostic accuracy, and outcomes in two high-risk patient populations.

ABSTRACT
The cure of blood diseases, such as sickle cell disease (SCD), requires using healthy donor (allogeneic)
hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) or genetically modified self-HSC. Toxic chemotherapy or radiation (i.e.,
conditioning) is required to deplete existing stem cells and make space for new cells. If the donor immune system
(graft) is not matched to the recipient (host), potentially fatal graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) will develop.
There is approximately a 10% mortality rate from conditioning and GVHD in the first 100 days after HSC
transplantation (HSCT). This means that those who can access allogeneic HSCT are limited to health-care
intensive countries and traditionally must have a matched donor, which is only ~30% for certain U.S. groups.
Gene therapy, i.e., the personalized correction of one’s own cells, currently utilizes ex vivo viral transduction or
electroporation of HSC. This then requires conditioning to remove the diseased HSCs that remain in the body
before gene corrected cells can be returned. Current gene therapy utilizes suboptimal methods, viral vectors or
electroporation, that cause cell toxicity and delayed engraftment. >10% of patients cannot provide enough HSC
for the current Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-cas9-based gene therapy
for SCD. The long-term objective of developing non-viral platforms for less toxic delivery to HSC is thus critical
for creating a new class of genetic medicines for blood disorders. To do this, nanoparticle (NP)-mediated delivery
of CRISPR-cas9 will be explored. In preliminary studies, Dr. Triebwasser has shown that poly(beta-amino ester)
(PBAE) polymeric NP carrying cas9 can efficiently edit primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells
(HSPC, CD34+ cells) with reduced toxicity compared to electroporation and without affecting erythropoiesis. The
central hypothesis is that PBAE cas9 NP gene editing of HSC has reduced toxicity compared to existing
methods (i.e., electroporation). In this grant, Dr. Triebwasser will deeply characterize the phenotype and
number of stem and progenitor cell subsets that are edited by PBAE NP using flow cytometry and single cell
RNA-seq. The function of gene-edited stem cells will be assessed with colony forming assays and
xenotransplantation (SA1). The ability of this NP platform to gene edit CD34+ cells from patients with SCD at the
clinically validated BCL11A +58 erythroid enhancer for gamma-globin reactivation will be assessed in vitro and
in vivo (SA2). Finally, chemical variants of this effective polymeric nanoparticle will be studied for improved
efficacy and stability (SA3), with in vivo studies in the future. By completing this experimental work under the

results.abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are essential for the continuous production and regeneration of the
hematopoietic system. Among them, long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) possess the unique ability
to self-renew and differentiate into all blood cell types, making them critical for maintaining blood homeostasis.
Leveraging the therapeutic potential of LT-HSCs, especially in the field of gene editing, holds great promise for
addressing genetic defects associated with various hematological disorders. Gene editing technologies, such as
CRISPR, have revolutionized molecular biology by enabling precise modifications of cell genetic material. In the
context of LT-HSCs, gene editing offers a potential solution for a wide range of hematological disorders, including
inherited blood diseases and malignancies. A significant application of gene editing in HSCs involves inducing
fetal hemoglobin (FH) production as a substitute for adult hemoglobin. Genetic mutations impacting the BCL11A
binding site on the γ-globin gene have demonstrated therapeutic potential for beta-hemoglobinopathies.
Currently, achieving FH induction in HSCs requires isolating CD34+ cells and applying CRISPR components ex
vivo through electroporation. However, this process is time-consuming, lacks specificity for LT-HSCs, and is
limited to well-equipped facilities, making it less accessible, particularly in resource-limited regions where most
cases of beta hemoglobinopathies occur. Additionally, patient HSCs may not be suitable for ex vivo treatment.
Thus, there is a critical need to develop in vivo CRISPR delivery systems to make this technology widely
available. Indeed, our preliminary data show that exosomes have highly specific interactions with long-term
hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs). Using a bottom-up nanotechnology approach we have developed
biomimetic LNPs that can encapsulate CRISPR in its highly effective RNP form. The proposed research is
innovative because it aims to investigate the potential of biomimetic CRISPR delivery vehicles, inspired by
exosomes that specifically interact with LT-HSCs, as gene editing delivery systems to induce FH production. By
incorporating highly specific exosome components, our Exo-CRISPR nanoformulations, can be engineered to
selectively target LT-HSCs. This approach offers the advantage of enhancing the efficiency and specificity of
CRISPR-based gene editing in LT-HSCs, maximizing therapeutic impact. Overall, this project aims to develop a
targeted and efficient gene editing delivery system using Exo-CRISPR LNPs to induce FH production, offering a
promising therapeutic strategy for beta hemoglobinopathies. The project's findings will contribute to advancing
the field of gene editing and improving the treatment outcomes for patients with hematopoietic disorders.

PROJECT NARRATIVE
Gene editing technologies, like CRISPR, hold great potential for treating genetic blood disorders by modifying
Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), particularly long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs). However, the
current ex vivo approach for gene editing is costly and limits accessibility, making the development of in vivo
CRISPR delivery vehicles crucial. Our biomimetic CRISPR delivery vehicle, inspired by exosomes (Exo-
CRISPR), offers a promising strategy to enhance the specificity and efficiency of gene editing in LT-HSCs,
providing a therapeutic avenue for beta hemoglobinopathies.

PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT
 Expression of erythroid-specific genes, including high level hemoglobin production, is established by lineage-
specific transcription factors with the help of more general co-factors such as chromatin remodeling complexes.
The BAF (Brahma-associated factor) multisubunit chromatin remodeler complex family consists of three main
subtypes and is required for chromatin accessibility and transcription of thousands of genes across most tissues
and cell types. Our preliminary data suggest that BAF complexes and their subunits differ in their roles during
erythroid development and display gene-selective functions at the clinically important b-hemoglobin gene locus.
Ablation of the BRG1 core catalytic component in human erythroid cell lines and primary cultures decreases
transcription of the fetal HBG globin genes but surprisingly spares the adult HBB gene. BRG1 is part of three
distinct complexes, canonical (CBAF), non-canonical (ncBAF) and polybromo (PBAF). In follow-up experiments,
we found that loss of ncBAF components accelerates erythroid differentiation and preferentially reduces
expression of fetal HBG and the minor adult globin HBD. The finding that a general regulatory complex can have
such specificity within a 5-gene locus is interesting in the broader understanding of the BAF complex, but also
clinically important since increasing the expression of both HBG and HBD would be beneficial in HBB disorders
such as sickle cell disease and b-thalassemia. In this proposal, we will dissect the molecular mechanisms by
which BAF subtypes and subunits are able to achieve such gene specificity. In Aim 1, we will dissect the scope
and mechanisms of ncBAF function in erythroid cells using acute loss of function approaches. In Aim 2, we will
extend these studies in vivo through knockout of the ncBAF subunit Brd9 in the mouse erythroid lineage. Finally
in Aim 3, we will extend our experiments to more closely define the roles of the other BAF subtypes in erythroid
maturation and hemoglobin regulation. This dissection of the surprising selectivity of the BAF subcomplexes may
provide new opportunities to therapeutically manipulate fetal hemoglobin for the treatment of sickle cell disease
(SCD) and b-thalassemias. Additionally, we hope to use the extensive tools and datasets developed in erythroid
systems to understand the function of BAF in other biological contexts such as malignancy.

Project Narrative
Understanding the mechanisms controlling red blood cell gene expression and hemoglobin production is
essential to developing new treatments for sickle cell disease and thalassemia. We have found that specific
subunits of the BAF chromatin regulator complex determine which genes can be activated by BAF, including
specific hemoglobin genes. In this proposal, we will study the mechanisms of BAF gene selectivity to identify
new ways to manipulate hemoglobin gene expression and treat red blood cell disorders.

results.abstract_text:
Oxidative stress mechanisms regulating g-globin gene transcription in sickle cell disease
Abstract:
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common inherited monogenic disorder affecting the β-globin
gene, leading to the production of sickled-shaped red blood cells (RBCs). Patients with SCD suffer from
severe anemia and painful vasoocclusive crises, which are both exacerbated by increased oxidative
stress. Induction of normal, but developmentally silenced γ-globin gene of fetal hemoglobin (HbF)
expression reduces RBC sickling-mediated vasoocclusion, and anemia, consequently ameliorating
clinical severity of SCD. Reducing oxidative stress also improves SCD phenotypic severity. Yet
effective treatment options remain limited. Understanding the pathogenesis of the erythroid
mechanisms regulating oxidative stress and factors engaged in silencing γ-globin gene, is of substantial
value to SCD patients. Our data uncovered an unanticipated role for mediators of oxidative stress in
RBC sickling, and in regulating the transcriptional regulatory machinery that represses γ-globin genes
as well as epigenetic enzyme components associated with γ-globin to β-globin gene switch in erythroid
progenitors. Here, to extend our studies, we will in vitro and in vivo genetically and/or chemically
manipulate these mediators of oxidative stress and the regulated pathways using a SCD mouse model,
and determine their effects on γ-globin gene regulation, and thus sickling, and their mechanism of
action on the transcriptional regulatory machinery that silences γ-globin gene during sickle RBC
production. We will also determine the contribution of these mediators in epigenetic DNA and histone
modifications associated with γ-globin
to β-globin gene switch during sickle RBC production. Because
stress erythropoiesis compensates for anemia caused by oxidative damage to the RBCs, we will further
validate the effects of these mediators of oxidative stress on stress erythropoiesis in splenic
hematopoietic tissue and examine their role in chronic erythroid stress-response, specifically in
erythroid terminal maturation and enucleation. We strongly believe that our studies will provide novel
and unprecedented insights into the exact mechanisms regulating γ-globin gene silencing and γ-globin
to β-globin gene switch in SCD, as well as ineffective erythroid maturation and enucleation. Our long-
term goal is to identify remediable sickle erythroid abnormalities to improve SCD pathophysiology. In
addition, our studies will lay the foundation for more rational approaches to therapies that better
alleviate SCD clinical symptoms.

Grant title: Role of CYB5R3 in erythropoiesis
Funding mechanism: NIH/NHLBI-F32
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3) plays a critical role in regulating redox signaling in both physiological
and pathological contexts. Key biological substrates of CYB5R3 include hemoproteins such as hemoglobin,
myoglobin, and soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), as well as vitamin E and coenzyme Q. Our recent findings
demonstrate that the CYB5R3 T117S variant, which results in approximately 50% loss of reductase activity,
serves as a modifier of hydroxyurea-induced fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production—a widely used therapeutic
approach for managing anemia in sickle cell disease (SCD). Using CYB5R3 knockout CD34+
hematopoietic stem cells (HSC)s, we found depleted baseline hemoglobin and impaired hydroxyurea-
induced HbF production and erythroid maturation. In CYB5R3-deleted human erythroleukemic K562 cells, we
similarly found depleted baseline hemoglobin, but in the presence of heme deficiency. The role of CYB5R3 in
erythropoiesis remains unexplored despite. Based on our preliminary and published data, we hypothesize
that CYB5R3 plays a previously unrecognized role in erythropoiesis by regulating heme biosynthesis. This
hypothesis will be tested using two specific aims: Aim 1 will investigate the impact of CYB5R3 depletion
on hemoglobin synthesis and erythropoiesis using human K562 cells. Aim 2 will employ a novel mouse
model with hematopoietic compartment-specific deletion of CYB5R3 to assess its effects on erythropoiesis
in vivo, both under baseline conditions and following hypoxic conditions. Successful completion of this
study will provide novel insights into the significance of CYB5R3 in erythropoiesis, with potential
applications in drug development, regenerative medicine, and the improved management of genetic
anemias. Moreover, this research—plan combined with mentored training under Drs. Straub and Wood,
interdisciplinary collaborations, and a structured career development plan within the outstanding
training environment at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine—will equip the applicant with the
expertise necessary to achieve a long-term career in biomedical research.

ABSTRACT
My long-term goal as a physician scientist is to contribute to our understanding of normal and abnormal
hematopoiesis and translate these findings into new treatments for patients with hematologic conditions. β-
hemoglobinopathies are the most common monogenic disorders in the world. They include sickle cell disease
(SCD) and β-thalassemia (β-thal), which are caused by defective or inadequate production of β-globin,
respectively. Current treatment options for these disorders have limited efficacy or remain inaccessible to most
patients. Reactivation of γ-globin, the β-like globin chain expressed during fetal development, results in
production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and reduces the clinical severity of SCD and β-thalassemia. Identification
of novel regulators of γ-globin could lead to the development of new therapies. In preliminary studies, we
performed a genome-scale CRISPR knockout screen to identify novel γ-globin repressors. This screen
identified several genes in the Spt-Ada-GCN5-acetyltransferase (SAGA) transcriptional regulatory complex as
candidate γ-globin repressors, including the transcriptional adaptor protein TADA2B. Genetic perturbation of
TADA2B results in a profound increase in γ-globin protein levels mediated at the transcriptional level. TADA2B
is required for full activity of the SAGA complex acetyltransferases KAT2A and KAT2B, and pharmacologic
protein degradation of KAT2A/B led to robust induction of γ-globin. In parallel, we performed a genome-scale
CRISPR activation screen for genes that positively regulate γ-globin production. Screening identified SKIL, a
regulator of TGF-β signaling, as an enhancer of γ-globin expression. Overexpression of SKIL resulted in
increased γ-globin protein production mediated at the transcriptional level. The aim of this project is to
determine the mechanism by which (1) TADA2B and (2) SKIL regulate γ-globin expression. This will be
accomplished through targeted genetic and pharmacologic studies in established in vitro and in vivo models of
normal human erythropoiesis and SCD. Results obtained from this proposal will enhance our understanding of
γ-globin regulation, which may lead to improved treatments for β-hemoglobinopathies. The research and
training plan will be supported by the excellent research and clinical environment at the University of Michigan
and will facilitate my development into an independent physician scientist focused on hematopoietic disorders.

ABSTRACT
Adults with SCD display remarkable variability in symptom presentation, despite the constancy of the HbS
mutation in the beta globin gene. Our team has long hypothesized that additional genetic variation beyond HbS
modulates this clinical variability. That hypothesis led to the establishment of the Outcome Modifying Genes in
SCD (OMG-SCD) cohort nearly 25 years ago to identify genetic modifiers of SCD. Over the years, we have
made seminal discoveries of genetic modifiers of many types of end organ damage (EOD) in adults with SCD,
including priapism, pulmonary hypertension, sickle cell nephropathy, bilirubin levels, fetal hemoglobin (HbF)
levels, acute chest syndrome, and painful vaso-occlusive crises. We also have identified genetic modifiers of
overall SCD severity, and our studies have shed light on the relationships between the progression of EOD and
early mortality. Nonetheless, as we recently reviewed, there are few modifiers (such as APOL1 and UGT1A1)
that have been reliably replicated across studies. The lack of replication for most SCD genetic modifiers has
likely been driven by two primary factors. 1) SCD is a rare disease and most genetic modifier studies have relied
on analysis of individual cohorts (including our own) with modest sample sizes and, thus, limited statistical power.
2) Most analytic approaches have employed standard GWAS analyses that do not harness additional statistical
power potentially realizable through newer methods. We now aim to overcome both these barriers. NHLBI’s
TOPMed program now includes several cross-sectional adult SCD cohorts (total N > 4000) with whole genome
sequencing (WGS) and extensive clinical data, such as information regarding EOD and overall disease severity.
Combining these clinical and genetic data with ancestry-aware and transcriptomic imputation analytic
approaches should significantly improve our statistical power for genetic modifier studies and thereby yield
important insights into the pathophysiologic processes contributing to EOD and overall SCD severity. Recent
methodologic improvements—such as new ancestry mapping methods and imputation of gene expression—have
become available but have not yet been applied to EOD or disease severity studies in SCD. Thus, both these
improvements open new and and novel opportunities for understanding the relationships between genetic and
genomic data and clinical variability in SCD. Our specific aims are to 1.) Determine the effect of local genomic
ancestry on EOD and disease severity in SCD and 2.) Evaluate the contribution of genetically-controlled gene
expression to EOD and disease severity in SCD. By uncovering genetic and transcriptomic determinants of
clinical variability in SCD, we expect to establish a foundation for future testing of precision medicine-guided
approaches to risk prediction and care models for SCD patients.

PROJECT NARRATIVE
Sickle cell disease results in significant organ damage and early mortality, with a mean life expectancy of only
58 years. We hypothesize that these effects of sickle cell disease are strongly determined by individual
variability in multiple ‘omics, such as genetics and transcriptomics, on organ systems such as the heart, lungs,
kidney and central nervous system. We will study the relationship of these multi-omics to individual organ
damage and overall disease severity, using the existing clinical and whole genome sequencing data from the
sickle cell disease cohorts (total >4000) deposited in the NHLBI TOPMed biodata repository, and apply new
ancestry-aware and transcriptomic imputation analytic methods.

results.abstract_text:
Project Summary
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a severe inherited blood disorder affecting over 100,000 individuals in the United States and millions globally. It is caused by a missense variant in the -globin gene that leads to hemoglobin S (HbS) polymerization, red blood cell (RBC) sickling, hemolysis, and downstream complications including vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs), stroke, and progressive organ damage. Fetal hemoglobin (HbF, ₂₂) inhibits HbS polymerization and is a well-established modifier of disease severity. Pharmacologic agents such as hydroxyurea (HU), and naturally occurring deletions in the -globin locus, such as those found in hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH), increase HbF and reduce clinical complications. However, many patients remain at risk for complications despite achieving high total HbF levels. Emerging data indicate that the distribution of HbF across individual RBCs, whether uniform (pancellular) or uneven (heterocellular), is a stronger determinant of clinical benefit than total HbF alone. The molecular mechanisms that govern this distribution remain poorly defined. This project will define how genetic and epigenetic regulation of -globin expression shapes HbF distribution and modifies disease severity in SCD. The central hypothesis is that red cell–intrinsic regulation of -globin determines HbF distribution, and that variation in this regulation underlies persistent clinical heterogeneity among patients with elevated HbF. Aim 1 will use single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin accessibility profiling, and genome editing to identify and functionally validate regulatory elements that control HbF distribution in individuals with naturally occurring -globin locus deletions, including HPFH and A-thalassemia. Aim 2 will study HU-treated patients with sustained high HbF levels but divergent clinical outcomes. By integrating single-cell RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, whole genome sequencing, and clinical phenotyping from multicenter cohorts, this aim will identify cell-intrinsic regulators associated with differential clinical outcomes. Functional studies in patient-derived erythroid cells will test whether candidate variants and pathways alter HbF distribution. This work addresses a critical gap in SCD management by identifying mechanisms of incomplete therapeutic response and biomarkers of residual risk. Findings will support precision HbF–inducing strategies and the rational development of combination therapies to reduce disease burden in children and adults with SCD.

results.phr_text:
Project Narrative
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a life-threatening inherited disorder marked by pain, organ damage, and reduced life expectancy. This project will define how genetic and epigenetic mechanisms control the distribution of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) across red blood cells and how this contributes to differences in clinical outcomes among patients with similar HbF levels. These insights will guide more precise prediction of disease severity and the development of improved therapies for individuals with SCD.

results.abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY
The production of red blood cells (RBC), known as ‘erythropoiesis’, serves as a paradigm for understanding
cellular differentiation and terminal maturation. Defects in erythropoiesis or RBC function cause various forms of
anemia, a health burden affecting nearly one-third of the global population. Each step of erythropoiesis, including
lineage specification, proliferation, differentiation, and terminal maturation into RBCs filled with hemoglobin for
oxygen transport, has unique metabolic requirements with potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention.
For instance, recent evidence indicates that hemoglobinopathies can be treated by stimulating glycolysis with
pyruvate kinase agonists. We demonstrated previously that glutamine synthesis is uniquely upregulated during
erythropoiesis to detoxify ammonium generated by heme synthesis and that enhanced glutamine synthetase
activity alleviates -thalassemia. However, the comprehensive metabolic regulation of erythropoiesis remains
poorly understood, which limits therapeutic opportunities. To address this knowledge gap, we performed global
metabolomic profiling, isotope tracing and transcriptome analysis of staged erythroid precursors from mouse
fetal liver and bone marrow. We discovered that distinct, ontogeny-specific metabolic processes govern
erythropoiesis. While glucose is the primary nutrient for bioenergetics and biosynthesis in fetal liver erythroid
precursors, mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) becomes more active during postnatal bone marrow
erythropoiesis. Surprisingly, isotope tracing showed that long chain fatty acids are essential metabolic precursors
for TCA cycle intermediates and heme during adult-type erythropoiesis. Moreover, genetic disruption of FAO
enzymes caused impaired erythropoiesis and anemia in adult mice, whereas erythroid FAO was profoundly
dysregulated in sickle cell disease (SCD). These findings support our central hypotheses that FAO provides
essential nutrients to support erythropoietic energy demands and biosynthetic needs, including heme
biosynthesis, and that dysfunctional FAO contributes to the pathophysiology of SCD. Thus, the objective of this
project is to elucidate the functional and mechanistic roles of fatty acid metabolism as a new regulatory pathway
in erythropoiesis and RBC disorders according to three specific aims: 1) Define the functional roles of FAO in
erythropoiesis; 2) Elucidate the mechanistic roles of fatty acid metabolism in erythrocyte development and
function; and 3) Determine the role of fatty acid metabolism in the pathophysiology of sickle cell disease. Our
hypotheses and the feasibility of proposed studies are supported by extensive preliminary data combining
orthogonal, state-of-the-art metabolic and transcriptomic approaches with orthogonal mouse and human models
to analyze erythropoiesis in vivo. Now we will elucidate fatty acid metabolism as a critical metabolic regulator of
normal postnatal erythropoiesis and a potential therapeutic target for SCD.
results.project_title: Fatty Acid Metabolism in Normal and Pathological Erythropoiesis
results.phr_text:
NARRATIVE
We are studying the metabolic processes by which nutrients are utilized to form red blood cells. While mature
red blood cells rely entirely on glucose for energy, we discovered an unexpected, essential role for fatty acid
breakdown during red blood cell formation in the bone marrow. By elucidating this metabolic process further, we
aim to better understand normal red blood cell formation and develop new therapies for common forms of
anemia, including sickle cell disease.

results.abstract_text:
reeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder affecting 5–8% of pregnancies and is associated with placental dysfunction, inflammation, oxidative stress, and adverse neonatal hematologic outcomes, including anemia and impaired red blood cell (RBC) quality. Although umbilical cord blood hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) retain erythroid potential, placenta-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (pMSCs) that regulate fetal erythropoiesis may be functionally compromised in preeclampsia. The mechanisms by which placental disease alters the fetal erythroid niche and downstream RBC functional quality remain poorly understood. 
The overall objective of this project is to define how pMSCs from normotensive versus preeclamptic pregnancies regulate cord blood HSPC-driven erythropoiesis and RBC functional maturation. Our central hypothesis is that preeclampsia disrupts pMSC-mediated niche signaling, impairing erythroid progenitor amplification, terminal maturation, and RBC functional integrity, despite preservation of intrinsic erythroid programming within cord blood HSPCs. 
To test this hypothesis, we will pursue three aims. Aim 1 will determine how normotensive versus preeclamptic pMSCs regulate early erythroid commitment and progenitor amplification in cord blood CD34⁺ HSPCs. Aim 2 will define how disease-altered pMSCs affect terminal erythroid maturation, enucleation, and hemoglobin programming. Aim 3 will assess the functional quality and storage resilience of RBCs generated under normotensive versus preeclamptic niche conditions by evaluating deformability, fragility, membrane maturation, and metabolic stability. 
This project is innovative because it reframes preeclampsia as a disorder of developmental erythropoiesis and RBC quality rather than solely a maternal vascular disease. The proposed studies establish a human disease-informed stromal niche model that directly links placental pathology to erythroid maturation and transfusion-relevant RBC function. By integrating placental stromal biology with functional erythroid and RBC performance assays, this work will define mechanistic pathways connecting placental dysfunction to neonatal hematologic vulnerability. 
The expected outcomes of this work are the identification of pMSC-mediated mechanisms governing fetal erythropoiesis and the determination of how preeclampsia impairs RBC maturation and quality. These findings are expected to advance understanding of placental disease biology and support development of stromal-supported perinatal RBC manufacturing strategies relevant to neonatal transfusion medicine, blood disorders, and regenerative hematology.
results.project_title: Placental Stromal Niche Regulation of Fetal Erythropoiesis and Red Blood Cell Quality in Preeclampsia

Impact. This study will define how preeclampsia alters the fetal erythroid niche, identify pMSC-mediated 
mechanisms that govern erythropoiesis, and determine whether disease-associated defects can be 
bypassed ex vivo. The results will advance the biology of placental preeclamptic disease and support the 
development of perinatal cell-based RBC manufacturing platforms relevant to neonatal transfusion and 
regenerative medicine.
